claim: The pre-Bötzinger Complex (preBötC) drives inspiration.
source: Breathing results from the interaction of two distinct oscillators: the pre-Bötzinger Complex (preBötC), which drives inspiration; and the lateral parafacial region (pFRG), which drives active expiration.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The lateral parafacial region (pFRG) drives active expiration.
source: Breathing results from the interaction of two distinct oscillators: the pre-Bötzinger Complex (preBötC), which drives inspiration; and the lateral parafacial region (pFRG), which drives active expiration.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The pFRG is silent at rest.
source: The pFRG is silent at rest and becomes rhythmically active during the stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors, which also activates adrenergic C1 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing no AbdEMG activity at baseline.

claim: The pFRG becomes rhythmically active during the stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors.
source: The pFRG is silent at rest and becomes rhythmically active during the stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors, which also activates adrenergic C1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing AbdEMG activity after KCN injection and hypoxia exposure.

claim: Peripheral chemoreceptor stimulation activates adrenergic C1 cells.
source: The pFRG is silent at rest and becomes rhythmically active during the stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors, which also activates adrenergic C1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by fos expression data showing C1 neuron activation during hypoxia.

claim: C1 neurons are activated by hypoxia.
source: We found in rats that: a) C1 neurons are activated by hypoxia and project to the pFRG region
evidence: This is supported by fos immunoreactivity data showing increased fos+ cells among C1 neurons (fos+/TH+) during hypoxia (158 ± 11, vs. 14 ± 3 for normoxia; p<0.001).

claim: C1 neurons project to the pFRG region.
source: We found in rats that: a) C1 neurons are activated by hypoxia and project to the pFRG region
evidence: This is supported by anterograde tracing with PRSx8-ChR2-eYFP showing GFP-labeled terminals in the pFRG and retrograde tracing with CTb showing labeled C1 neurons.

claim: Active expiration elicited by hypoxia was blunted after blockade of ionotropic glutamatergic receptors at the level of the pFRG.
source: b) active expiration elicited by hypoxia was blunted after blockade of ionotropic glutamatergic receptors at the level of the pFRG
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that bilateral Kyn injections into the pFRG completely eliminated the AE generated by AbdEMG induced by hypoxia (0.000 ± 0.000 mV vs. 0.386 ± 0.080 mV for saline+KCN; p<0.001).

claim: Selective depletion of C1 neurons eliminated the active expiration elicited by hypoxia.
source: c) selective depletion of C1 neurons eliminated the active expiration elicited by hypoxia.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that depletion of catecholaminergic neurons in the RVLM blunted AbdEMG activity elicited by KCN (0.000 ± 0.000 mV vs. 0.386 ± 0.08 mV for saline; p<0.05).

claim: C1 cells may regulate the respiratory cycle, including active expiration, under hypoxic conditions.
source: These results suggest that C1 cells may regulate the respiratory cycle, including active expiration, under hypoxic conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Breathing is a complex and dynamic behavior divided into three phases: inspiration, post-inspiration and active expiration.
source: Therefore, the process of breathing is a complex and dynamic behavior divided into three phases (inspiration, post-inspiration and active expiration), whereby respiratory muscles produce a pressure difference allowing airflow into and out of the lungs (Richter and Smith, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: There is a hypothesized third oscillator located at the post-inspiratory complex (PiCO) which drives the post-inspiratory phase of the breathing cycle.
source: There is a hypothesized third oscillator located at the post-inspiratory complex (PiCO) which drives the post-inspiratory phase of the breathing cycle (Del Negro et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Respiration influences the cardiovascular system through Traube-Hering waves and respiratory sinus arrhythmia.
source: Respiration influences the cardiovascular system through two different mechanisms: Traube-Hering waves, which are related to oscillations in arterial pressure, and the respiratory sinus arrhythmia, which is related to oscillation in the heart rate (Traube, 1865; Hering, 1869; Anrep et al., 1936; Machado et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The respiratory oscillators are located in the ventrolateral medulla, intermingled with neurons that are involved with cardiovascular control.
source: The respiratory oscillators are located in the ventrolateral medulla, intermingled with neurons that are involved with cardiovascular control (Guyenet, 2006; Richter and Smith, 2014; Guyenet, 2014; Machado et al., 2017; Del Negro et al., 2018), suggesting that they can interact to coordinate respiratory and cardiovascular adjustments.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM) contains many types of neurons that regulate the sympathetic and parasympathetic outflows as well as breathing output.
source: The rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM) contains many types of neurons that regulate the sympathetic and parasympathetic outflows as well as breathing output (Guyenet, 2006; Guyenet, 2014; Del Negro et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Catecholaminergic C1 neurons were first identified more than 40 years ago.
source: In the so-called 'cardiovascular/sympathetic' area of the RVLM, catecholaminergic C1 neurons were first identified more than 40 years ago (McAllen and Dampney, 1990; Guyenet, 2006; Guyenet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as historical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: C1 neurons have distinct projections to the whole brain.
source: C1 neurons have distinct projections to the whole brain, demonstrating that these neurons are involved in more than just cardiovascular regulation, as had been previously described (Ross et al., 1981; Li and Guyenet, 1996; Schreihofer and Guyenet, 1997; Ritter et al., 1998; Marina et al., 2011; Abbott et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Selective stimulation of C1 cells causes a rise in arterial pressure and breathing activity.
source: Selective stimulation of C1 cells causes a rise in arterial pressure and breathing activity (Abbott et al., 2013b; Burke et al., 2014; Malheiros-Lima et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The effects of C1 cell stimulation mimic the cardiovascular and respiratory responses elicited by hypoxia.
source: These effects mimic the cardiovascular and respiratory responses elicited by hypoxia (Burke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: C1 cells are highly collateralized and overlap with respiratory neurons in the VRC.
source: There is evidence that C1 cells are highly collateralized, overlap with respiratory neurons in the VRC and contribute to hypoxic responses via connections with pontomedullary structures (Guyenet, 2006; Guyenet, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hypoxia is considered a very potent stimulus that produces different physiological perturbations, including breathing activation.
source: Hypoxia is considered a very potent stimulus that produces different physiological perturbations, including breathing activation (Guyenet, 2000; Prabhakar and Semenza, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: During a hypoxic challenge, expiration turns into an active process with recruitment of abdominal expiratory muscles.
source: During a hypoxic challenge, expiration (which is passive at rest) turns into an active process, with dilatation of the upper airways and the recruitment of abdominal expiratory muscles during the second phase of the expiratory process (Iscoe, 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A group of expiratory neurons located in the parafacial respiratory group (pFRG) has been considered to be a conditional expiratory oscillator.
source: A group of expiratory neurons located in the parafacial respiratory group (pFRG) has been considered to be a conditional expiratory oscillator (Janczewski and Feldman, 2006; Pagliardini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The pFRG is located ventrolateral to the facial motor nucleus.
source: The pFRG is located ventrolateral to the facial motor nucleus and becomes rhythmically active when it is necessary to increase lung ventilation, for example during physical exercise or during the stimulation of central and/or peripheral chemoreceptors (Pagliardini et al., 2011; Huckstepp et al., 2015; Korsak et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The pFRG becomes rhythmically active when it is necessary to increase lung ventilation, for example during physical exercise or during the stimulation of central and/or peripheral chemoreceptors.
source: The pFRG is located ventrolateral to the facial motor nucleus and becomes rhythmically active when it is necessary to increase lung ventilation, for example during physical exercise or during the stimulation of central and/or peripheral chemoreceptors (Pagliardini et al., 2011; Huckstepp et al., 2015; Korsak et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Under resting conditions, expiration occurs passively as a consequence of the passive deflation of the lung and chest wall.
source: Under resting conditions, expiration occurs passively as a consequence of the passive deflation of the lung and chest wall to a resting state from a stretched position at the end of inspiration (Figure 1D–E and H).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Active expiration corresponds to an increase in the airflow in the late expiratory phase, immediately before inspiration, that is due to the recruitment of expiratory muscles.
source: Physiologically, active expiration (high ventilatory demand) corresponds to an increase in the airflow in the late expiratory phase, immediately before inspiration, that is due to the recruitment of expiratory muscles.
evidence: This is stated as a definition supported by citations.

claim: Active expiration is present when the abdominal (AbdEMG) amplitude during the final 20% of the expiratory period is >50% larger than that in the first half.
source: According to others, active expiration is present when the abdominal (AbdEMG) amplitude during the final 20% of the expiratory period is >50% larger than that in the first half (Figure 1D–E) (Pagliardini et al., 2011; Zoccal et al., 2018; Silva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological definition supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: In adult rats, the pFRG region is inactive at rest.
source: In adult rats, the pFRG region (a conditional expiratory oscillator) is inactive at rest and can became rhythmically active as a result of changes in the balance of inhibition and excitation, which recruit abdominal muscles by local disinhibition or activation (Janczewski and Feldman, 2006; Pagliardini et al., 2011; Huckstepp et al., 2015; Huckstepp et al., 2016; Huckstepp et al., 2018; Zoccal et al., 2018; Silva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The pFRG can become rhythmically active as a result of changes in the balance of inhibition and excitation.
source: In adult rats, the pFRG region (a conditional expiratory oscillator) is inactive at rest and can became rhythmically active as a result of changes in the balance of inhibition and excitation, which recruit abdominal muscles by local disinhibition or activation (Janczewski and Feldman, 2006; Pagliardini et al., 2011; Huckstepp et al., 2015; Huckstepp et al., 2016; Huckstepp et al., 2018; Zoccal et al., 2018; Silva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: C1 neurons use glutamate as the main neurotransmitter.
source: Considering the ideas that pFRG neurons are involved in active expiration and that C1 neurons use glutamate as the main neurotransmitter, we began by confirming that the activation of ionotropic glutamatergic receptors in pFRG neurons is able to generate active expirations (Huckstepp et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Unilateral injection of glutamate into the pFRG triggered active expiration.
source: Unilateral injection of glutamate into the pFRG triggered active expiration, as noted by bursts of AbdEMG during late expiration (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Glutamate injected into the pFRG elicited an increase in DiaEMG amplitude (0.771 ± 0.16 mV vs. baseline of 0.264 ± 0.068 mV; p<0.05).
source: For example, glutamate injected into the pFRG elicited an increase in DiaEMG amplitude (0.771 ± 0.16 mV vs. baseline of 0.264 ± 0.068 mV; p<0.05) and AbdEMG (0.236 ± 0.045 mV vs. baseline of 0.000 ± 0.000 mV; p<0.05) (Figure 1D–E and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Glutamate injected into the pFRG elicited an increase in AbdEMG (0.236 ± 0.045 mV vs. baseline of 0.000 ± 0.000 mV; p<0.05).
source: For example, glutamate injected into the pFRG elicited an increase in DiaEMG amplitude (0.771 ± 0.16 mV vs. baseline of 0.264 ± 0.068 mV; p<0.05) and AbdEMG (0.236 ± 0.045 mV vs. baseline of 0.000 ± 0.000 mV; p<0.05) (Figure 1D–E and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The injection of glutamate into the pFRG did not evoke an increase in the DiaEMG frequency (47 ± 7 bpm vs. baseline of 38 ± 6 bpm, p>0.05).
source: The injection of glutamate into the pFRG did not evoke an increase in the DiaEMG frequency (47 ± 7 bpm vs. baseline of 38 ± 6 bpm, p>0.05) or blood pressure (127 ± 8 mmHg vs. baseline of 120 ± 7 mmHg; p>0.05) (Figure 1D–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The injection of glutamate into the pFRG did not evoke an increase in blood pressure (127 ± 8 mmHg vs. baseline of 120 ± 7 mmHg; p>0.05).
source: The injection of glutamate into the pFRG did not evoke an increase in the DiaEMG frequency (47 ± 7 bpm vs. baseline of 38 ± 6 bpm, p>0.05) or blood pressure (127 ± 8 mmHg vs. baseline of 120 ± 7 mmHg; p>0.05) (Figure 1D–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Previous ipsilateral injection of Kyn into the pFRG completely abolished the active expiration generated by glutamate injections (0.000 ± 0.000 mV vs. 0.236 ± 0.045 mV with glutamate but no Kyn; p<0.05).
source: Previous ipsilateral injection of Kyn into the pFRG completely abolished the active expiration generated by glutamate injections (0.000 ± 0.000 mV vs. 0.236 ± 0.045 mV with glutamate but no Kyn; p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Blockade of the ionotropic glutamatergic receptors at the level of the pFRG did not affect the resting DiaEMG frequency (38 ± 5 bpm vs. 47 ± 7 bpm with active glutamatergic receptors; p>0.05).
source: Blockade of the ionotropic glutamatergic receptors at the level of the pFRG did not affect the resting DiaEMG frequency (38 ± 5 bpm vs. 47 ± 7 bpm with active glutamatergic receptors; p>0.05), DiaEMG amplitude (0.314 ± 0.114 mV vs. 0.771 ± 0.16 mV with active glutamatergic receptors; p>0.05) or blood pressure (124 ± 7 mmHg vs. 127 ± 8 mmHg with active glutamatergic receptors; p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Blockade of the ionotropic glutamatergic receptors at the level of the pFRG did not affect the resting DiaEMG amplitude (0.314 ± 0.114 mV vs. 0.771 ± 0.16 mV with active glutamatergic receptors; p>0.05).
source: Blockade of the ionotropic glutamatergic receptors at the level of the pFRG did not affect the resting DiaEMG frequency (38 ± 5 bpm vs. 47 ± 7 bpm with active glutamatergic receptors; p>0.05), DiaEMG amplitude (0.314 ± 0.114 mV vs. 0.771 ± 0.16 mV with active glutamatergic receptors; p>0.05) or blood pressure (124 ± 7 mmHg vs. 127 ± 8 mmHg with active glutamatergic receptors; p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Blockade of the ionotropic glutamatergic receptors at the level of the pFRG did not affect blood pressure (124 ± 7 mmHg vs. 127 ± 8 mmHg with active glutamatergic receptors; p>0.05).
source: Blockade of the ionotropic glutamatergic receptors at the level of the pFRG did not affect the resting DiaEMG frequency (38 ± 5 bpm vs. 47 ± 7 bpm with active glutamatergic receptors; p>0.05), DiaEMG amplitude (0.314 ± 0.114 mV vs. 0.771 ± 0.16 mV with active glutamatergic receptors; p>0.05) or blood pressure (124 ± 7 mmHg vs. 127 ± 8 mmHg with active glutamatergic receptors; p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Catecholaminergic and glutamatergic terminals are present at the level of the parafacial respiratory group.
source: Catecholaminergic and/or glutamatergic terminals and fibers were observed lateral to the caudal edge of the facial nucleus, a region described as a conditional expiratory oscillator (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Within the pFRG, several neurons (NeuN+) are in close contact with TH+ and/or VGlut2+ terminals.
source: Within the pFRG, we observed several neurons (NeuN+) in close contact with TH+ and/or VGlut2+ terminals located lateral to the caudal tip of the facial nucleus (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Injections of the lentivirus PRSx8-ChR2-eYFP into the left C1 region produced intense fluorescence protein expression only in neurons.
source: Injections of the lentivirus PRSx8-ChR2-eYFP into the left C1 region produced intense fluorescence protein expression only in neurons (Figure 3A, 3C and 3C').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: TH+/eYFP+ neurons were always located in close proximity to the original injection site and were concentrated in the region of the ventrolateral reticular formation that lies below the caudal end of the facial motor nucleus and extends up to 500 μm posterior to this level (−11.6 to −12.8 mm caudal to bregma).
source: These neurons (TH+/eYFP+) were always located in close proximity to the original injection site and were concentrated in the region of the ventrolateral reticular formation that lies below the caudal end of the facial motor nucleus and extends up to 500 μm posterior to this level (−11.6 to −12.8 mm caudal to bregma; Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical mapping data shown in Figure 3.

claim: On average, 56 ± 3% of the TH+ neurons were immunoreactive for GFP.
source: On average, 56 ± 3% of the TH+ neurons were immunoreactive (ir) for GFP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Transduced catecholaminergic neurons had putative catecholaminergic and glutamatergic varicosities within the pFRG.
source: Transduced catecholaminergic neurons had putative catecholaminergic and glutamatergic varicosities within the pFRG (Figures 2, 3D–H, E' and H').
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Every pontomedullary region that harbors noradrenergic neurons, including the locus coeruleus and the A1, A2 and A5 regions, also have GFP-labeled fibers.
source: We also noticed that every pontomedullary region that harbors noradrenergic neurons, including the locus coeruleus and the A1, A2 and A5 regions, also have GFP-labeled fibers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical mapping data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: C1 neurons have moderately dense projections to the nucleus of the solitary tract.
source: We observed (1) light projections within the raphe nucleus, a region also noted for its role in respiratory control; (2) moderately dense projections to the nucleus of the solitary tract, which receives input from the carotid bodies and other cardiopulmonary afferents; and (3) extremely dense projections to the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, medullary raphe and RTN (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical mapping data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: C1 neurons have extremely dense projections to the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, medullary raphe and RTN.
source: We observed (1) light projections within the raphe nucleus, a region also noted for its role in respiratory control; (2) moderately dense projections to the nucleus of the solitary tract, which receives input from the carotid bodies and other cardiopulmonary afferents; and (3) extremely dense projections to the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, medullary raphe and RTN (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical mapping data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: All projections from C1 neurons had a strong ipsilateral predominance.
source: All projections had a strong ipsilateral predominance.
evidence: This is stated based on anatomical observations.

claim: From a total of 129 ± 11 TH-ir cells in the C1 region, 107 ± 10 neurons project to the pFRG, representing 83% of the TH cells in the C1 region.
source: For example, from a total of 129 ± 11 TH-ir cells in the C1 region, we found that 107 ± 10 neurons project to the pFRG, representing 83% of the TH cells in the C1 region (Figure 4C and E).
evidence: This is supported by retrograde tracing and cell counting data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Few double-labeled cells (49 ± 4 vs. total TH: 148 ± 9; 33% of TH cells in the A2 region) were found within the cNTS.
source: As expected, CTb expression was also observed in cell bodies located in the commissural aspect of the nucleus of the solitary tract (cNTS); however, few double-labeled cells (49 ± 4 vs. total TH: 148 ± 9; 33% of TH cells in the A2 region) were found within the cNTS (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This is supported by retrograde tracing and cell counting data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Hypoxia caused a large increase in the number of fos+ cells among presumably pFRG neurons (fos+/TH–) compared to that in normoxia (115 ± 14, vs. 7 ± 2 for normoxia; p<0.001).
source: Hypoxia caused a large increase in the number of fos+ cells among presumably pFRG neurons (fos+/TH–) compared to that in normoxia (control group) (115 ± 14, vs. 7 ± 2 for normoxia; p<0.001) (Figure 5A–B and G).
evidence: This is supported by fos immunoreactivity data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Hypoxia caused a large increase in the number of fos+ cells among C1 neurons (fos+/TH+) (158 ± 11, vs. 14 ± 3 for normoxia; p<0.001).
source: As expected, we also detected a large number of fos+ cells among C1 neurons (fos+/TH+) (158 ± 11, vs. 14 ± 3 for normoxia; p<0.001) (Figure 5C–D and H).
evidence: This is supported by fos immunoreactivity data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The number of fos+ neurons in the cNTS (183 ± 8 vs. 10 ± 2 for normoxia; p<0.001) was higher in the hypoxia group than in the normoxia group.
source: The number of fos+ neurons in the cNTS (183 ± 8 vs. 10 ± 2 for normoxia; p<0.001) was higher in the hypoxia group than in the normoxia group (Figure 5E–F and I).
evidence: This is supported by fos immunoreactivity data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Bilateral Kyn injections into the pFRG did not change the increase in the DiaEMG frequency (58 ± 6 bpm vs. 71 ± 5 bpm for saline+KCN; p>0.05) induced by KCN.
source: Bilateral injections of Kyn into the pFRG did not change the increase in the DiaEMG frequency (58 ± 6 bpm vs. 71 ± 5 bpm for saline+KCN; p>0.05) induced by KCN (Figure 6D and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Blockade of ionotropic glutamatergic receptors in the pFRG reduced the DiaEMG amplitude (0.400 ± 0.163 mV vs. 1.714 ± 0.408 mV for saline+KCN; p<0.05) induced by KCN.
source: However, blockade of ionotropic glutamatergic receptors in the pFRG reduced the DiaEMG amplitude (0.400 ± 0.163 mV vs. 1.714 ± 0.408 mV for saline+KCN; p<0.05) and completely eliminated the AE generated by the AbdEMGinduced by hypoxia (0.000 ± 0.000 mV vs. 0.386 ± 0.080 mV for saline+KCN; p<0.001) (Figure 6D–E and G–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Blockade of ionotropic glutamatergic receptors in the pFRG completely eliminated the AE generated by the AbdEMG induced by hypoxia (0.000 ± 0.000 mV vs. 0.386 ± 0.080 mV for saline+KCN; p<0.001).
source: However, blockade of ionotropic glutamatergic receptors in the pFRG reduced the DiaEMG amplitude (0.400 ± 0.163 mV vs. 1.714 ± 0.408 mV for saline+KCN; p<0.05) and completely eliminated the AE generated by the AbdEMGinduced by hypoxia (0.000 ± 0.000 mV vs. 0.386 ± 0.080 mV for saline+KCN; p<0.001) (Figure 6D–E and G–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Kyn within the pFRG did not change the increase in AP elicited by KCN (142 ± 7 mmHg vs. 146 ± 9 mmHg for saline+KCN; p>0.05).
source: Kyn within the pFRG did not change the increase in AP elicited by KCN (142 ± 7 mmHg vs. 146 ± 9 mmHg for saline+KCN; p>0.05) (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Blockade of ionotropic glutamatergic receptors in the pFRG region did not change the increase in the DiaEMG frequency (54 ± 6 bpm vs. 68 ± 3 bpm for saline+KCN; p>0.05) induced by hypercapnia.
source: At the same time, blockade of ionotropic glutamatergic receptors in the pFRG region did not change the increase in the DiaEMG frequency (54 ± 6 bpm vs. 68 ± 3 bpm for saline+KCN; p>0.05) or the DiaEMG amplitude (0.543 ± 0.285 mV vs. 1 ± 0.234 mV for saline+KCN; p>0.05) but completely eliminated the AE generated by AbdEMG induced by hypercapnia (0.000 ± 0.000 mV vs. 0.271 ± 0.042 mV for saline+KCN; p<0.001) (Figure 6D and F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Blockade of ionotropic glutamatergic receptors in the pFRG region did not change the DiaEMG amplitude (0.543 ± 0.285 mV vs. 1 ± 0.234 mV for saline+KCN; p>0.05) induced by hypercapnia.
source: At the same time, blockade of ionotropic glutamatergic receptors in the pFRG region did not change the increase in the DiaEMG frequency (54 ± 6 bpm vs. 68 ± 3 bpm for saline+KCN; p>0.05) or the DiaEMG amplitude (0.543 ± 0.285 mV vs. 1 ± 0.234 mV for saline+KCN; p>0.05) but completely eliminated the AE generated by AbdEMG induced by hypercapnia (0.000 ± 0.000 mV vs. 0.271 ± 0.042 mV for saline+KCN; p<0.001) (Figure 6D and F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Blockade of ionotropic glutamatergic receptors in the pFRG region completely eliminated the AE generated by AbdEMG induced by hypercapnia (0.000 ± 0.000 mV vs. 0.271 ± 0.042 mV for saline+KCN; p<0.001).
source: At the same time, blockade of ionotropic glutamatergic receptors in the pFRG region did not change the increase in the DiaEMG frequency (54 ± 6 bpm vs. 68 ± 3 bpm for saline+KCN; p>0.05) or the DiaEMG amplitude (0.543 ± 0.285 mV vs. 1 ± 0.234 mV for saline+KCN; p>0.05) but completely eliminated the AE generated by AbdEMG induced by hypercapnia (0.000 ± 0.000 mV vs. 0.271 ± 0.042 mV for saline+KCN; p<0.001) (Figure 6D and F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Bilateral injections of Kyn into the pFRG did not change the increase in AP elicited by hypercapnia.
source: Bilateral injections of Kyn into the pFRG did not change the increase in AP elicited by hypercapnia (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the six rats treated with anti-DβH-SAP, the counts of TH-ir between −11.60 and −12.80 mm relative to bregma revealed an average depletion of 71 ± 3% (range between 61–80%).
source: In the six rats treated with anti-DβH-SAP, the counts of TH-ir between −11.60 and −12.80 mm relative to bregma revealed an average depletion of 71 ± 3% (range between 61–80%) (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 7.

claim: At the intermediate and caudal medullary levels (12.80 to −15.20 mm caudal to bregma), the number of TH-ir neurons was unaffected by treatment with anti-DβH-SAP (158 ± 7 neurons vs. 169 ± 10 neurons for saline; p>0.05).
source: At the intermediate and caudal medullary levels (12.80 to −15.20 mm caudal to bregma), the number of TH-ir neurons was unaffected by treatment with anti-DβH-SAP (158 ± 7 neurons vs. 169 ± 10 neurons for saline; p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data.

claim: The number of TH-ir neurons in the dorsal aspect of the medulla (A2 region) (307 ± 28 neurons vs. 331 ± 30 neurons for saline; p>0.05) did not differ after the anti-DβH-SAP treatment.
source: The number of TH-ir neurons in the dorsal aspect of the medulla (A2 region) (307 ± 28 neurons vs. 331 ± 30 neurons for saline; p>0.05) or in the ventrolateral pons (A5 region) (203 ± 24 neurons vs. 185 ± 15 neurons for saline; p>0.05) did not differ after the anti-DβH-SAP treatment.

claim: The number of TH-ir neurons in the ventrolateral pons (A5 region) (203 ± 24 neurons vs. 185 ± 15 neurons for saline; p>0.05) did not differ after the anti-DβH-SAP treatment.

claim: Selective ablation of catecholaminergic C1 neurons in the rostral ventrolateral medulla attenuated the late-expiratory flow and the late-E peak of AbdEMG activity observed during hypoxia in non-anesthetized rats.
source: We propose the existence of a catecholaminergic mechanism for the generation of active expiration because selective ablation of catecholaminergic C1 neurons in the rostral ventrolateral medulla attenuated the late-expiratory flow and the late-E peak of AbdEMG activity observed during hypoxia in non-anesthetized rats (Malheiros-Lima et al., 2017) and in anesthetized, vagotomized and artificially ventilated rats (present study).
evidence: This is stated as evidence from a previous study.

claim: Ablation of the C1 cells did not affect the generation of active expiration elicited by the activation of central chemoreceptors (hypercapnia condition).
source: This effect seems to be exclusive to the activation of peripheral chemoreceptors because ablation of the C1 cells did not affect the generation of active expiration elicited by the activation of central chemoreceptors (hypercapnia condition).

claim: The recruitment of abdominal muscles by chemosensory drives could be mediated through different neuromodulatory systems.

claim: The control of expiratory activity by C1 neurons is consistent with their function in increasing lung ventilation according to the intensity of the hypercapnic or hypoxic stimulus.
source: The control of expiratory activity by C1 neurons is consistent with their function in increasing lung ventilation according to the intensity of the hypercapnic or hypoxic stimulus (Guyenet and Bayliss, 2015; Pisanski and Pagliardini, 2019).

claim: Active expiration triggered by hypoxia depends on the integrity of C1 neurons located in the rostral aspect of the ventrolateral medulla.
